text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--- Denmark's police has now formed a specialist group of 12 experienced police officers to investigate crime commited by biker groups and coordinate with police authorities in the rest of Scandinavia.

--- The Danish customs and tax authorities' intensified fight to track down businesses which pay no tax has shown to be a success. In the first six months of 1996 the authorities collected 115 million crowns in unpaid taxes.
--- A major increase in child-care provisions will send local authority taxes up sharply next year, despite central government demands for a freeze.

--- A new survey from Denmark's working authorities shows that psychological problems caused by a bad working environment in Danish firms costs the Danish state 2.6 million crowns a year and that every day more than two Danes have to leave work permanently because of poor working conditions.

--- Danish GDP is expected to reach more than 1000 billion crowns in the second half of 1996, corresponding to about 200,000 crowns per Dane and places Denmark among the richest countries in the world.

--- A new survey from Greens Analysis institute of the economic trend in Denmark in the third quarter of 1996 shows that 13 percent of Danish companies are to hire more people. The need for more employees will mainly be in the sectors of finance and construction.
--- Increased French interest in wind energy could enlarge the market for Danish windmill manufacturers.
--- The opposition Conservatives say they do not intend to jointly negotiate on the 1997 draft state budget with their erstwhile Liberal allies.
